items: Stage flows, quiz and subscription coverage: agreed, all inside the current retainer. SMS I would only half switch off, because the campaigns and the flows are behaving very differently.

The stage problem is bigger than the three flows you named. From six months on the tracks earn $0.023 a recipient across 239,476 emails a quarter, which is campaign economics on your most personalised asset.

Cadence is the one I'd hold rather than cut. Your heaviest weeks carry the lowest unsubscribe rate (-0.54), and last quarter you sent 36% more and earned 27% more at a lower rate than the quarter before.
A cut to a quarter of the volume costs about $483.0k a year and on this data it would not move the unsubscribe rate.
blocks.label: The short of it

blocks.html:
The stage tracks

Right target, and the curve is steeper than the three flows you named: $0.377 a recipient at newborn, $0.0037 at twelve months.

blocks.cap: Nursing and pumping tracks combined, last 90 days.
blocks.title: What each stage earns, against what it sends

blocks.html:
Months zero to five: 219,464 emails a quarter at $0.206 a recipient. Months six to twelve: 239,476 at $0.023. Over half the stage volume goes to mums whose need has largely passed, which is two different jobs.

Zero to five is a rebuild, and it is where your 17,500 new customers from July and August land. Six to twelve is a positioning question, because no rewrite sells lactation support to a mum who has started solids. Worth deciding what we sell that cohort before spending a day on the copy.

Order: zero to two, then three to five, then a decision on six to twelve. They go into the same testing cadence as everything else, so each one gets a control and a variant rather than one rewrite and hope.

Cadence: I would hold it

Sends per week against the unsubscribe rate is -0.54: busier weeks run a lower rate per recipient, and the five worst weeks of the year were all one and two send weeks. Cadence drives the unsubscribe count (+0.64) only because it drives volume.

The last two quarters ran the test. To Jun ’26: 44 campaigns, $138.6k, $0.018 a recipient, 0.191% unsubscribes. To Aug ’26: 60 campaigns, up 36%, $175.4k, up 27%, at $0.023 and 0.183%. More sending, better per recipient, lower rate.

With growth taken out, sends against revenue per campaign is -0.17, so a single campaign earns no less as volume rises. Cutting to a quarter would take about $483.0k of revenue with it.

blocks.cap: Last six months. Bars are campaigns sent, the area is campaign revenue, the line is revenue per recipient.
blocks.title: Campaigns sent, what they earned, and what each recipient was worth

blocks.html:
What I would add rather than subtract is more blog campaigns. In the category report in this tab, blog sends returned the most revenue per send of any category and targeted sends the least, because a targeted send reaches a fraction of the people. Since you are billed per email, revenue per send is the number that decides this, not revenue per recipient.

Happy to stage-target the blog pieces where the subject suits it, but I would not narrow the audience to do it. A piece on sleep regression is still worth reading for a mum whose baby is past it, and worth forwarding to the friend whose baby is not.

blocks.cap: 52 weeks, grouped by campaigns per week. Bars are what the week earned, the line is the unsubscribe rate per recipient.
blocks.title: Revenue and unsubscribe rate at each cadence you have run

blocks.html:
Where the unsubscribes come from

Campaigns carry the volume, 67,130 over twelve months against 11,563 from flows. Per email delivered it reverses: 0.60% on flows against 0.23% on campaigns.

No single campaign is doing it. Across 81 sends the rate runs 0.108% to 0.294%, median 0.183%, worst one 2.4% of the total. Nor is there a suppression win left: campaigns already go to a 90-day engaged segment with seven exclusion lists on top, not the 678,522-profile file.

If anything the audience is too tight. About 53,277 people opened or clicked something in the last three to six months but sit outside the 90-day window, so they receive no campaigns at all. They are warm, they are already yours, and nothing is going to them. That is who the evergreen flow below is for.

blocks.cap: Each bar is one campaign. The line is the median at 0.183%.
blocks.title: Every campaign's unsubscribe rate, last 120 days

blocks.cap: Last three months. The two halves of the channel behave nothing alike.
blocks.title: SMS revenue: flows against campaigns

blocks.html:
Quiz, subscriptions, SMS

Quiz. $3.54 a recipient, reaching 10,855 people in 90 days. Into the welcome series and post-purchase, then test it as a campaign.

Subscriptions. Upcoming Charge earns $3.03 a recipient, second only to the quiz. On the 4,728 against roughly 12,000 orders a month: those two do not compare, because that flow can only reach people who are on a subscription. Loop fired 5,407 upcoming-order events last quarter and the flow delivered to 4,694 of them, so coverage is already about 87% and there is no trigger fault to fix.

That moves the subscription ask somewhere more useful. Subscription orders run about 1,127 a month against roughly 10,200 orders in total, one in nine. Last quarter Loop started 2,644 subscriptions and cancelled 2,233, so the base is barely growing. The expansion worth building is the cancel, skip and failed-payment side, plus the push from first order onto subscription, rather than more reach on a flow already reaching nearly everyone eligible.

SMS. Half agreed. Your $1.4k is the campaign side, and yes, switch that off until we rebuild it: at 1.63% unsubscribes it is paying to lose people. The SMS flows are a different channel wearing the same name, and they earned $18.5k over the same three months. I would stop the SMS campaigns and leave the automations running.

One addition. An evergreen best-of flow. Your ten best campaigns averaged $0.031 a recipient against a $0.022 median at 0.201% unsubscribes. On a flow that content keeps earning, and it gives us something to send those 53,277 warm people. It is also the natural place to test the quiz: a best-of flow going to people we do not otherwise reach is a free shot at putting the quiz in front of far more of them. It will pull the flow average per recipient down, since it is campaign content on a flow rail. The revenue is still additional.

Cost. Nothing extra, all inside the current rate. Let's look at scope again in six months once the stage tracks are rebuilt.
